title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
description: Compare blocking vs non-blocking, reliability, and complexity of sync and async communication.

data.text: Synchronous communication blocks the caller until a response arrives. Asynchronous communication lets the caller continue and handle the response later. Each has trade-offs in reliability, latency, and complexity.

terms.definition: The caller waits for the response before continuing.
The caller continues and handles the response via callback or event.
Middleware that routes messages between services asynchronously.
The ability of a system to handle when producers are faster than consumers.

items: Response handled later via callback or event
Synchronous: User-facing requests needing immediate response

data.text: Asynchronous systems are more complex: you need message brokers, idempotency, dead letter queues, and monitoring. But they offer better resilience and scalability for high-throughput systems.

data.title: Exercise: Design Communication Flows
data.description: For an e-commerce checkout flow, decide which steps are synchronous and which are asynchronous.

Classify each step as sync or async
Justify each choice based on user experience and reliability
data.expectedOutcome: A classified list and sequence diagram with justifications

items.question: When should I avoid async communication?
items.answer: When the user needs an immediate response, like reading a profile or checking availability.

items.question: What is the main risk of async?
items.answer: Complexity: message loss, duplication, ordering, and debugging distributed flows.

items.question: Can I mix sync and async?
items.answer: Yes, most systems do. Use sync for queries and async for commands and events.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Sync for immediate responses, async for resilience and throughput
Async adds complexity but improves availability
Most systems use a mix of both
data.takeaway: Use sync for user-facing queries and async for background processing and events.
